title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: TikTok trend
drivers.evidence: No past evidence of social media driving sales; effect shrunk to 1.0 due to single occurrence and no track record.

drivers.name: Price increase
drivers.evidence: 2.1% increase; no historical evidence of price sensitivity; noise-adjusted effect negligible.

drivers.name: Thanksgiving prep (week before)
drivers.evidence: Target week is 6 weeks after Thanksgiving; seasonal ramp is complete; baseline has absorbed this.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 9.0. No event is scheduled, but a price increase to $2.91 (+2.1%) may slightly dampen demand. The product trended on TikTok, but this is a single, unverified signal with no historical precedent. The classical uplift model suggests +23% from Thanksgiving prep, but that week is one week prior to the target. The target week is 6 weeks after Thanksgiving, well past the seasonal peak. Past promotions show no lasting lift, and the ordinary week after a promotion shows no rebound. The noise-adjusted effect of TikTok is uncertain and unvalidated. The price increase is minor and unlikely to drive a meaningful drop. The model’s suggested uplift is overstated for this timing. No driver justifies a move from 1.0.

  shelf price: 2.91 (+2.1% vs regular price 2.85)
  planner notes: Product is trending on TikTok

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 9.0 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 20.6 | 10%-90%: 1.3 - 17.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-81% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
